A Chinese revolutionary who led the Chinese Communist Party to power and founded the People's Republic of China in 1949. He ruled it until his death in 1976. His policies unified and rebuilt the country, and also caused the deadliest famine in history.

The son of a well-off peasant in Hunan, he was drawn to Marxism after the May Fourth Movement and helped found the Communist Party in 1921. When the Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek turned on the Communists, Mao built a base among peasants rather than city workers, a break with Soviet teaching. The Long March of 1934 to 1935 made him the party's leader. After fighting Japan, the Communists won the civil war, and Mao proclaimed the People's Republic on 1 October 1949.

His rule in brief:

  • Land reform, which killed many landlords, and the Korean War against the United States.
  • The Great Leap Forward of 1958 to 1962, a drive to overtake Britain in steel and farm output through people's communes. It led to the Great Chinese Famine, with tens of millions dead.
  • The Cultural Revolution from 1966, in which he set Red Guards against party leaders, teachers and old culture.
  • A break with the Soviet Union, and in 1972 a meeting with US President Nixon.

China under Mao raised literacy and life expectancy and built heavy industry, but stayed poor. After his death, Deng Xiaoping dismantled much of his economic system. The party's official verdict of 1981 held that his achievements outweighed his mistakes, a judgement often summed up as 70 percent right and 30 percent wrong. His portrait still hangs over Tiananmen Square.
